Hello, Doctor. Well, to tell you the truth, what brings me in is I just don’t have the push I used to have anymore. It’s like my get-up-and-go just got up and left, you know? I used to be so busy all the time. Take my choir, for instance. I’ve been singing with them for years and years, every Wednesday night practice and Sunday morning service, but lately, I just can't bring myself to get dressed and go out the door for it. And my quilting, too. I had this big basket of fabric scraps all cut out for a star pattern quilt I was making, just lovely little calico prints, but it's just sitting there in the living room corner gathering dust now. I don't even have the energy to thread a needle. 

I used to love visiting folks, going over to see my neighbors and having a cup of coffee, but now... well, most days I just sit at home. I sit right there in my chair with the TV on, but I keep it on real low. I don't even really watch the programs, it's just sort of flickering there with the volume barely a whisper while I sit. And the thing is, I know people are expecting me. The choir director keeps wondering where I am, and my friends are waiting on me to come visit like I used to, but I just stay in that chair with the TV turned down. I just can't seem to find the push for any of it anymore, no matter how much I know I ought to be doing things.

Well, I suppose that goes right back to what I was saying about the choir and my quilting, doesn't it? It's not that I don't like them anymore. I mean, I love my choir. I've got my robe hanging right there in the closet, the blue one with the gold trim around the collar. We had them specially made about five years ago because the old burgundy ones were getting so frayed at the cuffs. And I love the hymns we sing. "How Great Thou Art" is my absolute favorite, especially when we get to the chorus and the sopranos really let loose. I've always been an alto myself, holding down the harmony. 

And the quilting, too. I picked out those fabrics so carefully. I went all the way over to the JoAnn's two towns over just to find the perfect shade of buttercup yellow for the center of the stars. I spent hours washing and ironing and cutting those little pieces. I used to get such a thrill out of matching up the points perfectly. My grandmother taught me how to quilt when I was just a girl, and I've always found such peace in the rhythm of the needle going in and out. 

So it's not that I don't care for those things anymore, doctor. I still think they're wonderful things to do. It's just... I just don't have the spark for them right now. The thought of getting up, getting dressed, driving to the church, standing there for an hour and a half... or even just pulling the quilt frame over to my chair and threading the needle... it just feels like climbing a mountain. So I sit there. I look at the quilt basket, and I know I should enjoy it, I know I *used* to enjoy it, but the feeling of wanting to actually *do* it just isn't there. It's like the starter motor is broken, even though the engine is perfectly fine. Does that make sense? I haven't lost my love for them, just the... the doing of them.

Two years... well, yes, I suppose it has been right about that long. You see, this whole... whatever you want to call it, this paused feeling I was just telling you about, it really started building up right after I retired from the school office. And that was a little over two years ago now.

They had a sheet cake with buttercream frosting—the good kind, not that whipped stuff—and they gave me a beautiful engraved clock. But after that... well, the first few weeks were nice, getting to sleep in past six o'clock, but then the days just started stretching out. At first, I thought I was just catching my breath after all those years of the morning rush, but the catching my breath turned into sitting, and the sitting just kept going. So it's been building up ever since then, month by month, just slowly draining out until here I am, two years later, just sitting in my chair with the TV turned down.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose that goes right back to what I was saying about the choir and my quilting, doesn't it? It's not that I don't like them anymore. I mean, I love my choir. I've got my robe hanging right there in the closet, the blue one with the gold trim around the collar. We had them specially made about five years ago because the old burgundy ones were getting so frayed at the cuffs. And I love the hymns we sing. \"How Great Thou Art\" is my absolute favorite, especially when we get to the chorus and the sopranos really let loose. I've always been an alto myself, holding down the harmony. \n\nAnd the quilting, too. I picked out those fabrics so carefully. I went all the way over to the JoAnn's two towns over just to find the perfect shade of buttercup yellow for the center of the stars. I still think they're wonderful things to do. It's just... I just don't have the spark for them right now. It's like the starter motor is broken, even though the engine is perfectly fine. Does that make sense? I haven't lost my love for them, just the... the doing of them.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling depressed or down most of the day, nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was trying to explain just a moment ago, doctor, I wouldn't call it depressed or down. So I don't have to worry about paying my electric bill or buying my groceries, which is a comfort. Depressed? Down? Well... no, I wouldn't use those words. I really wouldn't. It's funny you ask it that way, because my daughter, Susan—the dental hygienist in Grand Rapids I mentioned—she called me just last Sunday. She usually calls on Sundays right after she gets back from the grocery store, around two o'clock. Anyway, she was asking me the exact same thing. She said, "Mom, are you depressed?" And I told her exactly what I'm telling you. 

I'm not sad, doctor. I don't sit in my living room crying or feeling sorry for myself. I don't look out the window at the rain and feel gloomy. It's not a sadness. It's just... well, it's just this heavy stillness. This lack of wanting to do anything. Like the battery has been taken out of a clock. The clock isn't sad that it's not ticking, it just... isn't ticking. 

I remember when my husband passed away, back in 1992. Now that was sadness. That was a terrible, heavy sadness that sat on my chest like a boulder. I cried every day for months. I would walk past his favorite armchair—the brown corduroy one that we finally had to give to the Goodwill because the springs were completely shot—and I would just break down right there in the hallway. That was feeling down. I know what that feels like, and I can tell you for a certainty that what I've been feeling these past two years since my retirement is not that. 

It's just that I don't see the point in getting up and making a fuss anymore. I don't want to go to the store, I don't want to chat with Mrs. Gable over the fence, I don't want to bake those oatmeal raisin cookies I used to make for the school bake sales. But it's not because I'm depressed. It's just... I'm done. The doing part of me is just finished. So no, I haven't had any stretches where I felt depressed or down. Not at all.

Well, yes, I suppose you could say that. But it's not like I actively dislike those things now. It's more like... well, let me explain. I used to sing in the church choir. First Presbyterian, right on the corner of Elm and 4th. I was an alto. Sang with them for, oh, must be twenty-five years. And visiting folks, too. I'd always be the first one over with a casserole if someone was sick or had a new baby. A tuna noodle casserole with the crushed potato chips on top—that was my specialty. 

But now... I just don't have the push I used to have for any of it. The choir director, Mr. Thomas—he's a very patient man, always wears those little wire-rimmed glasses—he's called a few times to ask where I've been. So it's been building up ever since then, month by month, just slowly draining out until here I am, two years later, just sitting in my chair with the TV turned down.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose that goes right back to what I was saying about the choir and my quilting, doesn't it? It's not that I don't like them anymore. I mean, I love my choir. I've got my robe hanging right there in the closet, the blue one with the gold trim around the collar. We had them specially made about five years ago because the old burgundy ones were getting so frayed at the cuffs. And I love the hymns we sing. \"How Great Thou Art\" is my absolute favorite, especially when we get to the chorus and the sopranos really let loose. I've always been an alto myself, holding down the harmony. \n\nAnd the quilting, too. I picked out those fabrics so carefully. I went all the way over to the JoAnn's two towns over just to find the perfect shade of buttercup yellow for the center of the stars. I spent hours washing and ironing and cutting those little pieces. I used to get such a thrill out of matching up the points perfectly. My grandmother taught me how to quilt when I was just a girl, and I've always found such peace in the rhythm of the needle going in and out. \n\nSo it's not that I don't care for those things anymore, doctor. I still think they're wonderful things to do. It's just... I just don't have the spark for them right now. The thought of getting up, getting dressed, driving to the church, standing there for an hour and a half... or even just pulling the quilt frame over to my chair and threading the needle... it just feels like climbing a mountain. So I sit there. I look at the quilt basket, and I know I should enjoy it, I know I *used* to enjoy it, but the feeling of wanting to actually *do* it just isn't there. It's like the starter motor is broken, even though the engine is perfectly fine. Does that make sense? I haven't lost my love for them, just the... the doing of them.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling depressed or down most of the day, nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was trying to explain just a moment ago, doctor, I wouldn't call it depressed or down. I mean, people use those words so much these days, don't they? You turn on the daytime television—which I've been doing a lot of lately, just having it on in the background, mostly the game shows, 'The Price is Right' and such, though I don't really watch them, I just listen to the bells ringing and the audience clapping—and every other commercial is about being depressed. They show those little animated clouds raining on people, or folks looking out of rainy windows looking just miserable. \n\nBut I'm not miserable, and I'm not sad, and I'm certainly not crying all day. I'm just... flat. Every day is just flat. From the time I wake up—usually around seven-thirty, though sometimes I just lie there until nine because, well, what's the rush, you know? The bed is warm, and I have that heavy comforter my sister sent me from Minnesota, the goose down one that keeps the draft out—from that time until I go to sleep, it's just this big, long stretch of nothingness. I don't feel down in the dumps, I just don't feel much of anything at all. So if you're asking if I'm walking around weeping and wailing every day, no, absolutely not. I'm just sitting here, day in and day out, feeling like someone unplugged me from the wall.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt hopeless most days?\n\nPatient: Hopeless? Oh, my, no. I wouldn't use a strong word like that at all. Hopeless makes it sound like... well, like I think the sky is falling, or like I'm sitting around thinking there's absolutely no future left for me. And that's just not true. I know perfectly well I have plenty of things to keep going for. \n\nI've got my pension from the school district, for one thing, and that comes in like absolute clockwork on the second Tuesday of every single month. They set it up with that direct deposit right before I retired, which really was a blessing because it means I don't have to put my heavy coat on and trudge all the way down to the First National Bank on Main Street—the one with the big green awning that flaps when it's windy, you know the one—especially when the sidewalks get all icy and treacherous in the wintertime. So I don't have to worry about paying my electric bill or buying my groceries, which is a comfort. And my sister in Minnesota, the one who sent the goose down comforter I was telling you about, she calls me every Sunday evening right after she finishes her supper, usually around six-thirty her time. She tells me all about her grandchildren and the weather up there. \n\nSo I know there are good things in the world, and I know I have security. I don't sit here wringing my hands thinking all is lost, doctor. I just... I just don't have the get-up-and-go to join in with the world right now. But knowing the world is there, and knowing it's perfectly fine... well, that means I'm not hopeless. I'm just... paused, I suppose you could say. Just sitting here on pause.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt this way most days for at least two years?\n\nPatient: Two years... well, yes, I suppose it has been right about that long. You see, this whole... whatever you want to call it, this paused feeling I was just telling you about, it really started building up right after I retired from the school office. And that was a little over two years ago now. \n\nI remember the exact timing perfectly because my last day was the Friday right before Memorial Day weekend. They had a little gathering for me in the teachers' lounge, with a big sheet cake from the grocery store—the kind with the thick white buttercream frosting that's almost too sweet, with the little frosting roses in the corners. They gave me a beautiful potted peace lily that's still sitting right there in my living room window. It's a very sturdy plant, which is a blessing since I haven't been watering it quite as faithfully as I ought to these days. \n\nAnyway, after that Friday, I didn't have to go back on Tuesday when the long weekend was over. At first, I just thought I was catching my breath, you know? After all those years of waking up at five-thirty in the morning, making sure the daily attendance sheets were printed out and the morning announcements were typed up nice and neat... I just thought my body was finally taking a well-deserved rest. I thought I was just enjoying not having to rush around. \n\nBut then the whole summer went by, and September rolled around. I remember hearing the school buses starting to go past my house again, with their heavy brakes squeaking at the stop sign right at the corner of Elm and Maple. I could hear them from my living room, and I realized I had just been sitting in my chair for months. And I just kept sitting there. \n\nSo, yes, doctor, it's been a little over two years of this. It didn't happen all at once, mind you. It wasn't like flipping a light switch off. It just sort of... settled over me, little by little, like dust gathering on a windowsill, ever since I packed up my desk at the school. It's just been building and building since that retirement party, until it got to where I am now.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any changes in your sleep lately?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Oh, my sleep is just fine. I haven't noticed any changes there at all, doctor. Like I was saying, I usually wake up around seven-thirty, though sometimes I just stay under that nice warm goose down comforter until nine or so. But it's not because I'm not sleeping, or because I'm waking up in the middle of the night staring at the ceiling. \n\nI know some people my age have terrible trouble with their sleep. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house right next door, the one with the overgrown hydrangeas that she really ought to have pruned back in the fall—she tells me she's up at all hours. Pacing the floors, drinking warm milk, reading magazines... she says she hasn't had a full night's rest since 1998. But I don't have that problem. \n\nWhen I go to bed, usually right after the ten o'clock local news finishes up—I like to watch the weather report, even though I don't go out much, just to see what the weatherman, Jim, has to say. He's been doing the weather on channel four for at least fifteen years now, always wears those bright, cheerful ties—anyway, once the news is over, I turn off the television, brush my teeth, and get into bed. And I sleep right through until the morning. No tossing, no turning, no bad dreams. Just a good, solid sleep, night after night, exactly the same as it's always been. So no, I wouldn't say there have been any changes in my sleep whatsoever. It's perfectly normal.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel like a failure or that you’re not good enough?\n\nPatient: A failure? Oh, heavens no. I don't feel like a failure at all. Why would I? I worked for the school district for thirty-two years, doctor. Thirty-two years of making sure those attendance records were perfectly straight, every single day. The principals—and I went through four of them in my time, starting with Mr. Henderson, who was a lovely man but terribly disorganized, always leaving his coffee cups on top of important files—they all knew they could count on me. \n\nI did my job, and I did it well, and I raised my daughter all by myself after my husband passed. She's a dental hygienist now, over in Grand Rapids. Has a lovely home with a big wrap-around porch and two golden retrievers. You don't raise a successful dental hygienist and keep a school office running like a top for three decades if you're a failure, or if you're not good enough. \n\nI know I have value. I know I did good work. The fact that I just sit in my chair now... well, that's just because my energy is gone, like I said. It's not because I'm sitting there thinking poorly of myself. I look at that peace lily they gave me, and I remember all the nice things they wrote in my retirement card. Mrs. Higgins, the second-grade teacher, wrote a whole paragraph about how I saved her from a panic attack during her first week when the copier jammed. So no, I certainly don't feel like a failure. I just feel... tired, I suppose. Just terribly, terribly tired of participating. But I know I was good enough when I was doing it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a stretch of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Depressed? Down? Well... no, I wouldn't use those words. I really wouldn't. It's funny you ask it that way, because my daughter, Susan—the dental hygienist in Grand Rapids I mentioned—she called me just last Sunday. She usually calls on Sundays right after she gets back from the grocery store, around two o'clock. Anyway, she was asking me the exact same thing. She said, \"Mom, are you depressed?\" And I told her exactly what I'm telling you. \n\nI'm not sad, doctor. I don't sit in my living room crying or feeling sorry for myself. I don't look out the window at the rain and feel gloomy. It's not a sadness. It's just... well, it's just this heavy stillness. This lack of wanting to do anything. Like the battery has been taken out of a clock. The clock isn't sad that it's not ticking, it just... isn't ticking. \n\nI remember when my husband passed away, back in 1992. Now that was sadness. That was a terrible, heavy sadness that sat on my chest like a boulder. I cried every day for months. I would walk past his favorite armchair—the brown corduroy one that we finally had to give to the Goodwill because the springs were completely shot—and I would just break down right there in the hallway. That was feeling down. I know what that feels like, and I can tell you for a certainty that what I've been feeling these past two years since my retirement is not that. \n\nIt's just that I don't see the point in getting up and making a fuss anymore. I don't want to go to the store, I don't want to chat with Mrs. Gable over the fence, I don't want to bake those oatmeal raisin cookies I used to make for the school bake sales. But it's not because I'm depressed. It's just... I'm done. The doing part of me is just finished. So no, I haven't had any stretches where I felt depressed or down. Not at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest or pleasure in the things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose you could say that. But it's not like I actively dislike those things now. It's more like... well, let me explain. I used to sing in the church choir. First Presbyterian, right on the corner of Elm and 4th. I was an alto. Sang with them for, oh, must be twenty-five years. We practiced every Wednesday evening at seven sharp, and we'd perform on Sundays. I used to love it, really I did. The harmonies, the fellowship... we'd always have coffee and those little shortbread cookies in the basement afterward. \n\nAnd my quilting! I was part of a circle that met at the community center. We made a beautiful double-wedding-ring quilt for the mayor's daughter when she got married back in 2018. It had these lovely pastel blues and yellows. I used to spend hours picking out the fabrics, cutting the squares perfectly, making sure every stitch was just right. I took real pride in it. \n\nAnd visiting folks, too. I'd always be the first one over with a casserole if someone was sick or had a new baby. A tuna noodle casserole with the crushed potato chips on top—that was my specialty. \n\nBut now... I just don't have the push I used to have for any of it. The choir director, Mr. Thomas—he's a very patient man, always wears those little wire-rimmed glasses—he's called a few times to ask where I've been. And the quilting ladies, they sent a very nice card. So I know people are expecting me. I know I should go. But most days, I just sit at home in my armchair. I keep the TV on low, usually tuned to one of those channels that plays old game shows, just for the background noise, really. \n\nI don't even watch it closely. I just sit there. The thought of getting dressed, driving over to the church, making small talk... it just feels like trying to move through molasses. The drive just isn't there anymore. So yes, I guess the interest is gone, but it's more that the energy to be interested is gone, if that makes any sense.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Ask about exactly ONE thing. Well, like I was saying before, doctor... no, I haven't been sad or down. I really haven't. It's just like I told my daughter, Susan, when she called on Sunday. I'm not sitting here crying all day. So I sit there. I look at the quilt basket, and I know I should enjoy it, I know I *used* to enjoy it, but the feeling of wanting to actually *do* it just isn't there. It's like the starter motor is broken, even though the engine is perfectly fine. Does that make sense? I haven't lost my love for them, just the... the doing of them.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling depressed or down most of the day, nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was trying to explain just a moment ago, doctor, I wouldn't call it depressed or down. I mean, people use those words so much these days, don't they? You turn on the daytime television—which I've been doing a lot of lately, just having it on in the background, mostly the game shows, 'The Price is Right' and such, though I don't really watch them, I just listen to the bells ringing and the audience clapping—and every other commercial is about being depressed. They show those little animated clouds raining on people, or folks looking out of rainy windows looking just miserable. \n\nBut I'm not miserable, and I'm not sad, and I'm certainly not crying all day. I'm just... flat. Every day is just flat. From the time I wake up—usually around seven-thirty, though sometimes I just lie there until nine because, well, what's the rush, you know? The bed is warm, and I have that heavy comforter my sister sent me from Minnesota, the goose down one that keeps the draft out—from that time until I go to sleep, it's just this big, long stretch of nothingness. I don't feel down in the dumps, I just don't feel much of anything at all. So if you're asking if I'm walking around weeping and wailing every day, no, absolutely not. I'm just sitting here, day in and day out, feeling like someone unplugged me from the wall.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt hopeless most days?\n\nPatient: Hopeless? Oh, my, no. I wouldn't use a strong word like that at all. Hopeless makes it sound like... well, like I think the sky is falling, or like I'm sitting around thinking there's absolutely no future left for me. And that's just not true. I know perfectly well I have plenty of things to keep going for. \n\nI've got my pension from the school district, for one thing, and that comes in like absolute clockwork on the second Tuesday of every single month. They set it up with that direct deposit right before I retired, which really was a blessing because it means I don't have to put my heavy coat on and trudge all the way down to the First National Bank on Main Street—the one with the big green awning that flaps when it's windy, you know the one—especially when the sidewalks get all icy and treacherous in the wintertime. So I don't have to worry about paying my electric bill or buying my groceries, which is a comfort. And my sister in Minnesota, the one who sent the goose down comforter I was telling you about, she calls me every Sunday evening right after she finishes her supper, usually around six-thirty her time. She tells me all about her grandchildren and the weather up there. \n\nSo I know there are good things in the world, and I know I have security. I don't sit here wringing my hands thinking all is lost, doctor. I just... I just don't have the get-up-and-go to join in with the world right now. But knowing the world is there, and knowing it's perfectly fine... well, that means I'm not hopeless. I'm just... paused, I suppose you could say. Just sitting here on pause.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt this way most days for at least two years?\n\nPatient: Two years... well, yes, I suppose it has been right about that long. You see, this whole... whatever you want to call it, this paused feeling I was just telling you about, it really started building up right after I retired from the school office. And that was a little over two years ago now. \n\nI remember the exact timing perfectly because my last day was the Friday right before Memorial Day weekend. They had a little gathering for me in the teachers' lounge, with a big sheet cake from the grocery store—the kind with the thick white buttercream frosting that's almost too sweet, with the little frosting roses in the corners. They gave me a beautiful potted peace lily that's still sitting right there in my living room window. It's a very sturdy plant, which is a blessing since I haven't been watering it quite as faithfully as I ought to these days. \n\nAnyway, after that Friday, I didn't have to go back on Tuesday when the long weekend was over. At first, I just thought I was catching my breath, you know? After all those years of waking up at five-thirty in the morning, making sure the daily attendance sheets were printed out and the morning announcements were typed up nice and neat... I just thought my body was finally taking a well-deserved rest. I thought I was just enjoying not having to rush around. \n\nBut then the whole summer went by, and September rolled around. I remember hearing the school buses starting to go past my house again, with their heavy brakes squeaking at the stop sign right at the corner of Elm and Maple. I could hear them from my living room, and I realized I had just been sitting in my chair for months. And I just kept sitting there. \n\nSo, yes, doctor, it's been a little over two years of this. It didn't happen all at once, mind you. It wasn't like flipping a light switch off. It just sort of... settled over me, little by little, like dust gathering on a windowsill, ever since I packed up my desk at the school. It's just been building and building since that retirement party, until it got to where I am now.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any changes in your sleep lately?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Oh, my sleep is just fine. I haven't noticed any changes there at all, doctor. Like I was saying, I usually wake up around seven-thirty, though sometimes I just stay under that nice warm goose down comforter until nine or so. But it's not because I'm not sleeping, or because I'm waking up in the middle of the night staring at the ceiling. \n\nI know some people my age have terrible trouble with their sleep. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house right next door, the one with the overgrown hydrangeas that she really ought to have pruned back in the fall—she tells me she's up at all hours. Pacing the floors, drinking warm milk, reading magazines... she says she hasn't had a full night's rest since 1998. But I don't have that problem. \n\nWhen I go to bed, usually right after the ten o'clock local news finishes up—I like to watch the weather report, even though I don't go out much, just to see what the weatherman, Jim, has to say. He's been doing the weather on channel four for at least fifteen years now, always wears those bright, cheerful ties—anyway, once the news is over, I turn off the television, brush my teeth, and get into bed. And I sleep right through until the morning. No tossing, no turning, no bad dreams. Just a good, solid sleep, night after night, exactly the same as it's always been. So no, I wouldn't say there have been any changes in my sleep whatsoever. It's perfectly normal.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel like a failure or that you’re not good enough?\n\nPatient: A failure? Oh, heavens no. I don't feel like a failure at all. Why would I? I worked for the school district for thirty-two years, doctor. Thirty-two years of making sure those attendance records were perfectly straight, every single day. The principals—and I went through four of them in my time, starting with Mr. Henderson, who was a lovely man but terribly disorganized, always leaving his coffee cups on top of important files—they all knew they could count on me. \n\nI did my job, and I did it well, and I raised my daughter all by myself after my husband passed. She's a dental hygienist now, over in Grand Rapids. Has a lovely home with a big wrap-around porch and two golden retrievers. I just feel... tired, I suppose. Just terribly, terribly tired of participating. But I know I was good enough when I was doing it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a stretch of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Depressed? Down? Well... no, I wouldn't use those words. I really wouldn't. It's funny you ask it that way, because my daughter, Susan—the dental hygienist in Grand Rapids I mentioned—she called me just last Sunday. She usually calls on Sundays right after she gets back from the grocery store, around two o'clock. Anyway, she was asking me the exact same thing. She said, \"Mom, are you depressed?\" And I told her exactly what I'm telling you. \n\nI'm not sad, doctor. I don't sit in my living room crying or feeling sorry for myself. I don't look out the window at the rain and feel gloomy. It's not a sadness. It's just... well, it's just this heavy stillness. This lack of wanting to do anything. Like the battery has been taken out of a clock. The clock isn't sad that it's not ticking, it just... isn't ticking. \n\nI remember when my husband passed away, back in 1992. Now that was sadness. That was a terrible, heavy sadness that sat on my chest like a boulder. I cried every day for months. I would walk past his favorite armchair—the brown corduroy one that we finally had to give to the Goodwill because the springs were completely shot—and I would just break down right there in the hallway. That was feeling down. I know what that feels like, and I can tell you for a certainty that what I've been feeling these past two years since my retirement is not that. \n\nIt's just that I don't see the point in getting up and making a fuss anymore. I don't want to go to the store, I don't want to chat with Mrs. Gable over the fence, I don't want to bake those oatmeal raisin cookies I used to make for the school bake sales. But it's not because I'm depressed. It's just... I'm done. The doing part of me is just finished. So no, I haven't had any stretches where I felt depressed or down. Not at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest or pleasure in the things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose you could say that. But it's not like I actively dislike those things now. It's more like... well, let me explain. I used to sing in the church choir. First Presbyterian, right on the corner of Elm and 4th. I was an alto. Sang with them for, oh, must be twenty-five years. We practiced every Wednesday evening at seven sharp, and we'd perform on Sundays. I used to love it, really I did. The harmonies, the fellowship... we'd always have coffee and those little shortbread cookies in the basement afterward. \n\nAnd my quilting! I was part of a circle that met at the community center. We made a beautiful double-wedding-ring quilt for the mayor's daughter when she got married back in 2018. It had these lovely pastel blues and yellows. I used to spend hours picking out the fabrics, cutting the squares perfectly, making sure every stitch was just right. I took real pride in it. \n\nAnd visiting folks, too. I'd always be the first one over with a casserole if someone was sick or had a new baby. A tuna noodle casserole with the crushed potato chips on top—that was my specialty. \n\nBut now... The choir director, Mr. Thomas—he's a very patient man, always wears those little wire-rimmed glasses—he's called a few times to ask where I've been. And the quilting ladies, they sent a very nice card. So I know people are expecting me. I know I should go. But most days, I just sit at home in my armchair. I keep the TV on low, usually tuned to one of those channels that plays old game shows, just for the background noise, really. \n\nI don't even watch it closely. I just sit there. The thought of getting dressed, driving over to the church, making small talk... it just feels like trying to move through molasses. The drive just isn't there anymore. So yes, I guess the interest is gone, but it's more that the energy to be interested is gone, if that makes any sense.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling sad or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was saying before, doctor... no, I haven't been sad or down. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Doctor, I feel like we're going around in circles a bit here. Are you sure you're listening to me? Because you keep asking about being sad or depressed, and now you're asking if it's been going on for two years. 

Well, two years ago is exactly when I retired from the packing plant. Thirty years I worked on that line, putting those little foam inserts into the cardboard shipping boxes. Thirty years. On my last day, they gave me a sheet cake in the breakroom—it was vanilla with that whipped icing, not the heavy buttercream, which I actually prefer, but it was a very nice thought—and a little glass plaque with my name engraved on it. That plaque sits right on my television stand now, right next to the framed picture of my husband from our trip to Mount Rushmore. 

And ever since that day, since that retirement party two years ago, I've just been... stopped. But not sad. I haven't been sitting here crying for two years, doctor. I haven't been depressed. I just sit in my chair. I watch Bob Barker—well, Drew Carey now, I suppose—on The Price is Right, I watch Let's Make a Deal, I watch the dust motes float around in the sunlight that comes through the front blinds. But I don't feel sad about it. I don't feel down. It's just how things are now. The factory whistle doesn't blow for me anymore, so I just stay put. 

So no, for the past two years, I have not been sad and I have not been depressed. I'm just parked. Like a car in a garage that nobody drives anymore. It's not a sad car, it's just not going anywhere.

So it's been building up ever since then, month by month, just slowly draining out until here I am, two years later, just sitting in my chair with the TV turned down.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose that goes right back to what I was saying about the choir and my quilting, doesn't it? It's not that I don't like them anymore. I mean, I love my choir. I've got my robe hanging right there in the closet, the blue one with the gold trim around the collar. We had them specially made about five years ago because the old burgundy ones were getting so frayed at the cuffs. And I love the hymns we sing. \"How Great Thou Art\" is my absolute favorite, especially when we get to the chorus and the sopranos really let loose. I've always been an alto myself, holding down the harmony. \n\nAnd the quilting, too. I picked out those fabrics so carefully. I went all the way over to the JoAnn's two towns over just to find the perfect shade of buttercup yellow for the center of the stars. I spent hours washing and ironing and cutting those little pieces. I used to get such a thrill out of matching up the points perfectly. My grandmother taught me how to quilt when I was just a girl, and I've always found such peace in the rhythm of the needle going in and out. \n\nSo it's not that I don't care for those things anymore, doctor. I still think they're wonderful things to do. It's just... I just don't have the spark for them right now. The thought of getting up, getting dressed, driving to the church, standing there for an hour and a half... or even just pulling the quilt frame over to my chair and threading the needle... it just feels like climbing a mountain. So I sit there. I look at the quilt basket, and I know I should enjoy it, I know I *used* to enjoy it, but the feeling of wanting to actually *do* it just isn't there. It's like the starter motor is broken, even though the engine is perfectly fine. Does that make sense? I haven't lost my love for them, just the... the doing of them.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling depressed or down most of the day, nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was trying to explain just a moment ago, doctor, I wouldn't call it depressed or down. I mean, people use those words so much these days, don't they? You turn on the daytime television—which I've been doing a lot of lately, just having it on in the background, mostly the game shows, 'The Price is Right' and such, though I don't really watch them, I just listen to the bells ringing and the audience clapping—and every other commercial is about being depressed. They show those little animated clouds raining on people, or folks looking out of rainy windows looking just miserable. \n\nBut I'm not miserable, and I'm not sad, and I'm certainly not crying all day. I'm just... flat. Every day is just flat. From the time I wake up—usually around seven-thirty, though sometimes I just lie there until nine because, well, what's the rush, you know? The bed is warm, and I have that heavy comforter my sister sent me from Minnesota, the goose down one that keeps the draft out—from that time until I go to sleep, it's just this big, long stretch of nothingness. I don't feel down in the dumps, I just don't feel much of anything at all. So if you're asking if I'm walking around weeping and wailing every day, no, absolutely not. I'm just sitting here, day in and day out, feeling like someone unplugged me from the wall.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt hopeless most days?\n\nPatient: Hopeless? Oh, my, no. I wouldn't use a strong word like that at all. Hopeless makes it sound like... well, like I think the sky is falling, or like I'm sitting around thinking there's absolutely no future left for me. And that's just not true. I know perfectly well I have plenty of things to keep going for. \n\nI've got my pension from the school district, for one thing, and that comes in like absolute clockwork on the second Tuesday of every single month. They set it up with that direct deposit right before I retired, which really was a blessing because it means I don't have to put my heavy coat on and trudge all the way down to the First National Bank on Main Street—the one with the big green awning that flaps when it's windy, you know the one—especially when the sidewalks get all icy and treacherous in the wintertime. So I don't have to worry about paying my electric bill or buying my groceries, which is a comfort. And my sister in Minnesota, the one who sent the goose down comforter I was telling you about, she calls me every Sunday evening right after she finishes her supper, usually around six-thirty her time. She tells me all about her grandchildren and the weather up there. \n\nSo I know there are good things in the world, and I know I have security. I don't sit here wringing my hands thinking all is lost, doctor. I just... I just don't have the get-up-and-go to join in with the world right now. But knowing the world is there, and knowing it's perfectly fine... well, that means I'm not hopeless. I'm just... paused, I suppose you could say. Just sitting here on pause.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt this way most days for at least two years?\n\nPatient: Two years... well, yes, I suppose it has been right about that long. You see, this whole... whatever you want to call it, this paused feeling I was just telling you about, it really started building up right after I retired from the school office. And that was a little over two years ago now. \n\nI remember the exact timing perfectly because my last day was the Friday right before Memorial Day weekend. They had a little gathering for me in the teachers' lounge, with a big sheet cake from the grocery store—the kind with the thick white buttercream frosting that's almost too sweet, with the little frosting roses in the corners. They gave me a beautiful potted peace lily that's still sitting right there in my living room window. It's a very sturdy plant, which is a blessing since I haven't been watering it quite as faithfully as I ought to these days. \n\nAnyway, after that Friday, I didn't have to go back on Tuesday when the long weekend was over. At first, I just thought I was catching my breath, you know? After all those years of waking up at five-thirty in the morning, making sure the daily attendance sheets were printed out and the morning announcements were typed up nice and neat... I just thought my body was finally taking a well-deserved rest. I thought I was just enjoying not having to rush around. \n\nBut then the whole summer went by, and September rolled around. I remember hearing the school buses starting to go past my house again, with their heavy brakes squeaking at the stop sign right at the corner of Elm and Maple. I could hear them from my living room, and I realized I had just been sitting in my chair for months. And I just kept sitting there. \n\nSo, yes, doctor, it's been a little over two years of this. It didn't happen all at once, mind you. It wasn't like flipping a light switch off. It just sort of... settled over me, little by little, like dust gathering on a windowsill, ever since I packed up my desk at the school. It's just been building and building since that retirement party, until it got to where I am now.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any changes in your sleep lately?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Oh, my sleep is just fine. I haven't noticed any changes there at all, doctor. Like I was saying, I usually wake up around seven-thirty, though sometimes I just stay under that nice warm goose down comforter until nine or so. But it's not because I'm not sleeping, or because I'm waking up in the middle of the night staring at the ceiling. \n\nI know some people my age have terrible trouble with their sleep. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house right next door, the one with the overgrown hydrangeas that she really ought to have pruned back in the fall—she tells me she's up at all hours. Pacing the floors, drinking warm milk, reading magazines... she says she hasn't had a full night's rest since 1998. He's been doing the weather on channel four for at least fifteen years now, always wears those bright, cheerful ties—anyway, once the news is over, I turn off the television, brush my teeth, and get into bed. And I sleep right through until the morning. No tossing, no turning, no bad dreams. Just a good, solid sleep, night after night, exactly the same as it's always been. So no, I wouldn't say there have been any changes in my sleep whatsoever. It's perfectly normal.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel like a failure or that you’re not good enough?\n\nPatient: A failure? Oh, heavens no. I don't feel like a failure at all. Why would I? I worked for the school district for thirty-two years, doctor. Thirty-two years of making sure those attendance records were perfectly straight, every single day. The principals—and I went through four of them in my time, starting with Mr. Henderson, who was a lovely man but terribly disorganized, always leaving his coffee cups on top of important files—they all knew they could count on me. \n\nI did my job, and I did it well, and I raised my daughter all by myself after my husband passed. She's a dental hygienist now, over in Grand Rapids. Has a lovely home with a big wrap-around porch and two golden retrievers. I had this big basket of fabric scraps all cut out for a star pattern quilt I was making, just lovely little calico prints, but it's just sitting there in the living room corner gathering dust now. I don't even have the energy to thread a needle. \n\nI used to love visiting folks, going over to see my neighbors and having a cup of coffee, but now... well, most days I just sit at home. I sit right there in my chair with the TV on, but I keep it on real low. I don't even really watch the programs, it's just sort of flickering there with the volume barely a whisper while I sit. And the thing is, I know people are expecting me. The choir director keeps wondering where I am, and my friends are waiting on me to come visit like I used to, but I just stay in that chair with the TV turned down. I just can't seem to find the push for any of it anymore, no matter how much I know I ought to be doing things.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel sad or down most of the day?\n\nPatient: Sad? Well... no. I wouldn't say that. It’s not a sadness, doctor. I mean, I know what sad is. Why, when my old dog Buster passed away—oh, it must be ten years ago now, he was a good little terrier mix, you know, the kind with the wiry hair that gets absolutely everywhere, on the rugs and the sofa cushions—I was just beside myself with sadness. I cried for days and days. I couldn't even look at his little red water bowl by the back door without tearing up and needing to sit down. Now, that’s being down. That's a heavy heart. \n\nBut this right now? It’s not like that at all. I don't feel like crying. I don't feel heartbroken or blue or... or any of those things people say when they're down in the dumps. It's just... well, it's just nothing, really. I'm not sitting in my chair weeping while the TV is on, I'm just sitting. The tears just aren't there, and that awful heavy feeling in your chest isn't there either. So no, I really wouldn't say I'm sad most of the day. It's more like the tank is just completely dry, if you catch my meaning. Just empty, not sad.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think back... it's been a while now. I suppose it really started to creep up on me after I finished up my time working at the school office. That was, oh, a little over two years ago now. I was the front desk secretary over at the elementary school, you see. I'd been there for thirty-four years, answering the phones and buzzing people in and putting Band-Aids on scraped knees when the nurse was at lunch. I knew every child's name, and every parent's name, and I always kept a big jar of peppermints right on the corner of my desk. We had them specially made about five years ago because the old burgundy ones were getting so frayed at the cuffs. Appetite? Well... no, I wouldn't say there's been a change, really. I mean, I eat what I've always eaten, just... maybe it takes me a little longer to get around to it. 

You see, I've always been a creature of habit when it comes to my meals. Every morning, for as long as I can remember—even back when I was working at the packing plant—I'd have a bowl of oatmeal. The Quaker Oats, not the instant kind in the little packets, but the old-fashioned oats that come in the cardboard cylinder with the smiling man on the front. I'd stand at the stove and stir it with a wooden spoon for exactly five minutes, and then I'd put a little pat of butter and a sprinkle of brown sugar on top. I still do that. I still make the oatmeal. 

And for lunch, it's usually half a sandwich. Tuna salad or maybe egg salad, depending on what I picked up at the Piggly Wiggly. I use that mayonnaise with the olive oil in it now, because Susan read an article in a magazine—Prevention, I think it was—that said it was better for your heart, though honestly I can't tell the difference in the taste. I eat the sandwich while I watch my programs. 

So the food is the same. The amount is the same. I just... I don't always feel the urge to get up out of the brown corduroy chair to go make it right at noon anymore. I'm not starving myself, doctor. I'm just... eating when I get around to it. So no, my appetite itself hasn't changed. Just the timing, I suppose.

Well, no, not at all. I’ve always been a very sound sleeper, doctor. Even back when I was working at the plant and had to be up before the sun, I’d sleep straight through until my alarm went off. But it's not because I'm depressed. It's just... I'm done. The doing part of me is just finished. So no, I haven't had any stretches where I felt depressed or down. Not at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest or pleasure in the things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose you could say that. But it's not like I actively dislike those things now. It's more like... well, let me explain. I used to sing in the church choir. First Presbyterian, right on the corner of Elm and 4th. I was an alto. Sang with them for, oh, must be twenty-five years. We practiced every Wednesday evening at seven sharp, and we'd perform on Sundays. I used to love it, really I did. The harmonies, the fellowship... we'd always have coffee and those little shortbread cookies in the basement afterward. \n\nAnd my quilting! I was part of a circle that met at the community center. We made a beautiful double-wedding-ring quilt for the mayor's daughter when she got married back in 2018. It had these lovely pastel blues and yellows. I used to spend hours picking out the fabrics, cutting the squares perfectly, making sure every stitch was just right. I took real pride in it. \n\nAnd visiting folks, too. I'd always be the first one over with a casserole if someone was sick or had a new baby. A tuna noodle casserole with the crushed potato chips on top—that was my specialty. \n\nBut now... I just don't have the push I used to have for any of it. The choir director, Mr. Thomas—he's a very patient man, always wears those little wire-rimmed glasses—he's called a few times to ask where I've been. And the quilting ladies, they sent a very nice card. So I know people are expecting me. I know I should go. But most days, I just sit at home in my armchair. I keep the TV on low, usually tuned to one of those channels that plays old game shows, just for the background noise, really. \n\nI don't even watch it closely. I just sit there. The thought of getting dressed, driving over to the church, making small talk... it just feels like trying to move through molasses. The drive just isn't there anymore. So yes, I guess the interest is gone, but it's more that the energy to be interested is gone, if that makes any sense.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling sad or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was saying before, doctor... no, I haven't been sad or down. I really haven't. It's just like I told my daughter, Susan, when she called on Sunday. I'm not sitting here crying all day. I'm not feeling sorry for myself. I don't wake up in the morning feeling this big heavy cloud of sadness over me, the way I did when my husband passed. \n\nI remember when he died, I'd wake up and before I even opened my eyes, I'd feel this terrible weight, like someone had stacked bricks on my chest while I was sleeping. And then I'd remember he was gone, and the tears would just start. I'd cry making coffee, I'd cry sorting the mail. I couldn't even look at his side of the closet for six months without breaking down. Now *that* was feeling sad most of the day, nearly every day. I know exactly what that feels like.\n\nBut this? This isn't that at all. I don't feel sad when I'm sitting in my chair with the game shows on. I don't feel down. I just don't feel... anything, really. I'm just sitting there. The day goes by—the mail carrier comes around eleven, usually, he's a nice young man named David, always makes sure the lid on the mailbox is shut tight so the rain doesn't get in—and I just watch the time pass. I'm not unhappy about it. I'm just empty of the desire to do anything else. So no, doctor, I wouldn't say I've been feeling sad or down at all. Just very, very still.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt sad or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, for most of the past two years?\n\nPatient: Doctor, I feel like we're going around in circles a bit here. Are you sure you're listening to me? Because you keep asking about being sad or depressed, and now you're asking if it's been going on for two years. \n\nWell, two years ago is exactly when I retired from the packing plant. Thirty years I worked on that line, putting those little foam inserts into the cardboard shipping boxes. Thirty years. On my last day, they gave me a sheet cake in the breakroom—it was vanilla with that whipped icing, not the heavy buttercream, which I actually prefer, but it was a very nice thought—and a little glass plaque with my name engraved on it. That plaque sits right on my television stand now, right next to the framed picture of my husband from our trip to Mount Rushmore. \n\nAnd ever since that day, since that retirement party two years ago, I've just been... stopped. But not sad. I haven't been sitting here crying for two years, doctor. I haven't been depressed. I just sit in my chair. I watch Bob Barker—well, Drew Carey now, I suppose—on The Price is Right, I watch Let's Make a Deal, I watch the dust motes float around in the sunlight that comes through the front blinds. But I don't feel sad about it. I don't feel down. It's just how things are now. The factory whistle doesn't blow for me anymore, so I just stay put. \n\nSo no, for the past two years, I have not been sad and I have not been depressed. I'm just parked. Like a car in a garage that nobody drives anymore. It's not a sad car, it's just not going anywhere.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling overly guilty about things or like you’ve let people down?\n\nPatient: Guilty? No, I wouldn't say that. I know you might think I should, what with missing the choir and the quilting circle and all. Susan—my daughter, you know—she asked me something similar just the other day. It was Wednesday, because I remember I had the weekly grocery circular spread out on my lap, looking to see if the chuck roast was on sale at the Piggly Wiggly while we were on the phone. She asked if I felt bad about not helping out with the church bake sale this year, since I usually make my famous lemon pound cake. \n\nBut I don't. I really don't feel bad about it. I did my time, doctor. Twenty-five years in that choir, thirty years at the packing plant making sure those foam inserts were perfectly straight. I've baked enough casseroles and sewn enough quilts to last a lifetime, I think. So I don't feel like I'm letting anyone down. \n\nThe choir has plenty of altos. Martha Higgins has been wanting to sing my parts for years anyway, even if she does tend to go a little flat on the high notes when she gets too excited. They're getting along just fine without me. And the quilting ladies, well, they have enough hands to finish whatever they're working on. I haven't done anything wrong by just sitting in my chair and resting. I'm just taking my rest now. So there's no guilt there, no. I don't feel guilty at all.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don’t feel sad, do you feel low or down inside most days?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I feel like I'm a bit of a broken record today. Low or down inside... no. I really don't. I know you're trying to get to the bottom of something here, asking it all these different ways, but I just don't have that feeling in me to give you. \n\nWhen I think of feeling low, I think of a sinking feeling, you know? Like... well, like back in '98 when the sump pump gave out and the basement flooded, and I went down the wooden stairs and saw all my husband's old National Geographic magazines just floating there in the muddy water. That gave me a real low feeling right here in my stomach. A heavy, sinking kind of feeling that just dragged on me. \n\nBut sitting in my house now? No, there's no sinking. There's no low. I'm just... resting. I sit in my recliner—it's one of those La-Z-Boys, the brown corduroy kind, very sturdy. My husband picked it out for me for our twenty-fifth anniversary because he knew my lower back used to ache terribly after standing on the concrete floor at the packing plant all day. He got a good deal on it at the Sears before it closed down. Anyway, I just sit in that brown chair, and I pull the little wooden handle to put the footrest up, and I look out the front window at the street, and I don't feel high and I don't feel low. I just feel perfectly flat. Just even. \n\nIt's like... like a calm pond where the water isn't moving at all, not even a ripple. So I can't say I feel down inside, doctor, because there's just no movement in there to go up or down in the first place. I'm just sitting.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any change in your appetite recently?\n\nPatient: Appetite? Well... no, I wouldn't say there's been a change, really. I mean, I eat what I've always eaten, just... maybe it takes me a little longer to get around to it. \n\nYou see, I've always been a creature of habit when it comes to my meals. Every morning, for as long as I can remember—even back when I was working at the packing plant—I'd have a bowl of oatmeal. The Quaker Oats, not the instant kind in the little packets, but the old-fashioned oats that come in the cardboard cylinder with the smiling man on the front. I'd stand at the stove and stir it with a wooden spoon for exactly five minutes, and then I'd put a little pat of butter and a sprinkle of brown sugar on top. I still do that. I still make the oatmeal. \n\nAnd for lunch, it's usually half a sandwich. Tuna salad or maybe egg salad, depending on what I picked up at the Piggly Wiggly. I use that mayonnaise with the olive oil in it now, because Susan read an article in a magazine—Prevention, I think it was—that said it was better for your heart, though honestly I can't tell the difference in the taste. I eat the sandwich while I watch my programs. \n\nSo the food is the same. The amount is the same. I just... I don't always feel the urge to get up out of the brown corduroy chair to go make it right at noon anymore. Sometimes it's one o'clock, or maybe two, before I finally pull the lever to put the footrest down and walk into the kitchen. But I still eat it. The food still tastes fine. I'm not starving myself, doctor. I'm just... eating when I get around to it. So no, my appetite itself hasn't changed. Just the timing, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: Have you been waking up earlier than usual or having trouble staying asleep?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not at all. I’ve always been a very sound sleeper, doctor. Even back when I was working at the plant and had to be up before the sun, I’d sleep straight through until my alarm went off. It was one of those old wind-up clocks, the metal ones with the two bells on top that make a terrible racket. But now, well, I don't need the clock anymore, so I don't set one. \n\nI usually head into the bedroom right after Wheel of Fortune finishes. I like to watch Pat and Vanna—she always wears such lovely gowns, though I wouldn't have anywhere to wear something like that myself, just sitting in the house. So right around seven-thirty or eight, I get up from my brown chair, wash my face with a warm washcloth, and get into bed. I have a very comfortable mattress. It’s a Sealy. Susan helped me pick it out about ten years ago because the old one was getting a terrible sag right in the middle where my husband used to lay, and it was doing no favors for my lower back. \n\nOnce I pull the covers up—I still use the double-wedding-ring quilt I made back in 1982, the one with the little scraps of blue gingham and yellow calico—I just close my eyes and that’s it. I don't toss, I don't turn. I don't wake up in the middle of the night to use the facilities or get a glass of water or worry about things. I just sleep. \n\nAnd as for waking up early, well, no. I don't do that either. I just sleep right on through until the light starts coming in through the curtains. They're heavy curtains, thermal ones, because the windows in that house can get a bit drafty in the winter, but a little light always peeks around the edges. Usually, it's about seven or maybe seven-thirty in the morning by the time I finally open my eyes. So I'm getting a full night's rest, really. Sometimes ten, eleven hours of just... nothing. Just quiet, heavy sleep. So no, I'm not having any trouble staying asleep or waking up before I'm supposed to. I just stay right there in the bed until I'm done resting.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling like a bad person or that you have very little worth lately?\n\nPatient: Well, no... no, I wouldn't say that. A bad person? No. I mean, I've always tried to do right by people. When I was working at the packing plant, I always did my fair share of the work on the line. I never slacked off or left a mess for the next shift to clean up, which is more than I can say for some of the girls who worked there. There was this one girl, Brenda... well, she was always sneaking off to the breakroom to smoke those long, thin cigarettes she liked, leaving the rest of us to pick up the slack. But I never did that. I worked hard. I raised my family. I went to church on Sundays, at least until my husband passed and the drive just got to be a bit much for me on my own. \n\nAnd as for having little worth... well, I don't know about that either. I mean, I don't feel like I'm out here changing the world or anything, but I don't feel worthless. I just... I just feel like I'm here. It's just... resting. It has its place. \n\nI suppose I feel a bit like that. I'm just in my house, watching my programs, eating my oatmeal when I get around to it. I don't feel like a bad person for it. I don't feel guilty. I'm not sitting there thinking I'm a terrible burden or that I've done something wrong. I just don't have those kinds of thoughts, doctor. Two weeks? Well, let me think on that... no. No, I don't believe I have. I mean, life hasn't always been a bowl of cherries, you understand. When my husband passed away—oh, it’s been a good number of years now—well, naturally I was grieving. Anyone would be. I just can't seem to find the push for any of it anymore, no matter how much I know I ought to be doing things.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel sad or down most of the day?\n\nPatient: Sad? Well... no. I wouldn't say that. It’s not a sadness, doctor. I mean, I know what sad is. Why, when my old dog Buster passed away—oh, it must be ten years ago now, he was a good little terrier mix, you know, the kind with the wiry hair that gets absolutely everywhere, on the rugs and the sofa cushions—I was just beside myself with sadness. I cried for days and days. I couldn't even look at his little red water bowl by the back door without tearing up and needing to sit down. Now, that’s being down. That's a heavy heart. \n\nBut this right now? It’s not like that at all. I don't feel like crying. I don't feel heartbroken or blue or... or any of those things people say when they're down in the dumps. It's just... well, it's just nothing, really. I'm not sitting in my chair weeping while the TV is on, I'm just sitting. The tears just aren't there, and that awful heavy feeling in your chest isn't there either. So no, I really wouldn't say I'm sad most of the day. It's more like the tank is just completely dry, if you catch my meaning. Just empty, not sad.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think back... it's been a while now. I suppose it really started to creep up on me after I finished up my time working at the school office. That was, oh, a little over two years ago now. I was the front desk secretary over at the elementary school, you see. I'd been there for thirty-four years, answering the phones and buzzing people in and putting Band-Aids on scraped knees when the nurse was at lunch. I knew every child's name, and every parent's name, and I always kept a big jar of peppermints right on the corner of my desk. The kind with the red and white stripes, individually wrapped, because you have to be careful about germs in a school. \n\nWhen I retired, they threw me a lovely party in the cafeteria. They had a sheet cake with buttercream frosting—the good kind, not that whipped stuff—and they gave me a beautiful engraved clock. But after that... well, the first few weeks were nice, getting to sleep in past six o'clock, but then the days just started stretching out. At first, I thought I was just catching my breath after all those years of the morning rush, but the catching my breath turned into sitting, and the sitting just kept going. So it's been building up ever since then, month by month, just slowly draining out until here I am, two years later, just sitting in my chair with the TV turned down.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose that goes right back to what I was saying about the choir and my quilting, doesn't it? It's not that I don't like them anymore. I mean, I love my choir. I've got my robe hanging right there in the closet, the blue one with the gold trim around the collar. We had them specially made about five years ago because the old burgundy ones were getting so frayed at the cuffs. And I love the hymns we sing. \"How Great Thou Art\" is my absolute favorite, especially when we get to the chorus and the sopranos really let loose. I've always been an alto myself, holding down the harmony. \n\nAnd the quilting, too. I picked out those fabrics so carefully. I went all the way over to the JoAnn's two towns over just to find the perfect shade of buttercup yellow for the center of the stars. I spent hours washing and ironing and cutting those little pieces. I used to get such a thrill out of matching up the points perfectly. My grandmother taught me how to quilt when I was just a girl, and I've always found such peace in the rhythm of the needle going in and out. \n\nSo it's not that I don't care for those things anymore, doctor. I still think they're wonderful things to do. It's just... I just don't have the spark for them right now. The thought of getting up, getting dressed, driving to the church, standing there for an hour and a half... or even just pulling the quilt frame over to my chair and threading the needle... it just feels like climbing a mountain. So I sit there. I look at the quilt basket, and I know I should enjoy it, I know I *used* to enjoy it, but the feeling of wanting to actually *do* it just isn't there. It's like the starter motor is broken, even though the engine is perfectly fine. Does that make sense? I mean, people use those words so much these days, don't they? I know perfectly well I have plenty of things to keep going for. \n\nI've got my pension from the school district, for one thing, and that comes in like absolute clockwork on the second Tuesday of every single month. They set it up with that direct deposit right before I retired, which really was a blessing because it means I don't have to put my heavy coat on and trudge all the way down to the First National Bank on Main Street—the one with the big green awning that flaps when it's windy, you know the one—especially when the sidewalks get all icy and treacherous in the wintertime. So I don't have to worry about paying my electric bill or buying my groceries, which is a comfort. She tells me all about her grandchildren and the weather up there. \n\nSo I know there are good things in the world, and I know I have security. Just sitting here on pause.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt this way most days for at least two years?\n\nPatient: Two years... well, yes, I suppose it has been right about that long. And that was a little over two years ago now. \n\nI remember the exact timing perfectly because my last day was the Friday right before Memorial Day weekend. They had a little gathering for me in the teachers' lounge, with a big sheet cake from the grocery store—the kind with the thick white buttercream frosting that's almost too sweet, with the little frosting roses in the corners. They gave me a beautiful potted peace lily that's still sitting right there in my living room window. It's a very sturdy plant, which is a blessing since I haven't been watering it quite as faithfully as I ought to these days. \n\nAnyway, after that Friday, I didn't have to go back on Tuesday when the long weekend was over. At first, I just thought I was catching my breath, you know? After all those years of waking up at five-thirty in the morning, making sure the daily attendance sheets were printed out and the morning announcements were typed up nice and neat... I just thought my body was finally taking a well-deserved rest. I thought I was just enjoying not having to rush around. \n\nBut then the whole summer went by, and September rolled around. I remember hearing the school buses starting to go past my house again, with their heavy brakes squeaking at the stop sign right at the corner of Elm and Maple. I could hear them from my living room, and I realized I had just been sitting in my chair for months. And I just kept sitting there. \n\nSo, yes, doctor, it's been a little over two years of this. It's just been building and building since that retirement party, until it got to where I am now.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any changes in your sleep lately?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Oh, my sleep is just fine. I haven't noticed any changes there at all, doctor. Like I was saying, I usually wake up around seven-thirty, though sometimes I just stay under that nice warm goose down comforter until nine or so. But it's not because I'm not sleeping, or because I'm waking up in the middle of the night staring at the ceiling. \n\nI know some people my age have terrible trouble with their sleep. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house right next door, the one with the overgrown hydrangeas that she really ought to have pruned back in the fall—she tells me she's up at all hours. Pacing the floors, drinking warm milk, reading magazines... she says she hasn't had a full night's rest since 1998. But I don't have that problem. \n\nWhen I go to bed, usually right after the ten o'clock local news finishes up—I like to watch the weather report, even though I don't go out much, just to see what the weatherman, Jim, has to say. He's been doing the weather on channel four for at least fifteen years now, always wears those bright, cheerful ties—anyway, once the news is over, I turn off the television, brush my teeth, and get into bed. And I sleep right through until the morning. No tossing, no turning, no bad dreams. Just a good, solid sleep, night after night, exactly the same as it's always been. So no, I wouldn't say there have been any changes in my sleep whatsoever. It's perfectly normal.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel like a failure or that you’re not good enough?\n\nPatient: A failure? Oh, heavens no. I don't feel like a failure at all. Why would I? I worked for the school district for thirty-two years, doctor. Thirty-two years of making sure those attendance records were perfectly straight, every single day. The principals—and I went through four of them in my time, starting with Mr. Henderson, who was a lovely man but terribly disorganized, always leaving his coffee cups on top of important files—they all knew they could count on me. \n\nI did my job, and I did it well, and I raised my daughter all by myself after my husband passed. She's a dental hygienist now, over in Grand Rapids. Has a lovely home with a big wrap-around porch and two golden retrievers. I know I did good work. The fact that I just sit in my chair now... well, that's just because my energy is gone, like I said. It's not because I'm sitting there thinking poorly of myself. I look at that peace lily they gave me, and I remember all the nice things they wrote in my retirement card. Mrs. Higgins, the second-grade teacher, wrote a whole paragraph about how I saved her from a panic attack during her first week when the copier jammed. So no, I certainly don't feel like a failure. I just feel... tired, I suppose. Just terribly, terribly tired of participating. But I know I was good enough when I was doing it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a stretch of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Depressed? We made a beautiful double-wedding-ring quilt for the mayor's daughter when she got married back in 2018. It had these lovely pastel blues and yellows. I'd always be the first one over with a casserole if someone was sick or had a new baby. A tuna noodle casserole with the crushed potato chips on top—that was my specialty. \n\nBut now... The choir director, Mr. Thomas—he's a very patient man, always wears those little wire-rimmed glasses—he's called a few times to ask where I've been.
