Susan helped me pick it out about ten years ago because the old one was getting a terrible sag right in the middle where my husband used to lay, and it was doing no favors for my lower back. \n\nOnce I pull the covers up—I still use the double-wedding-ring quilt I made back in 1982, the one with the little scraps of blue gingham and yellow calico—I just close my eyes and that’s it. I don't toss, I don't turn. I don't wake up in the middle of the night to use the facilities or get a glass of water or worry about things. I just sleep. \n\nAnd as for waking up early, well, no. I don't do that either. I just sleep right on through until the light starts coming in through the curtains. They're heavy curtains, thermal ones, because the windows in that house can get a bit drafty in the winter, but a little light always peeks around the edges. Usually, it's about seven or maybe seven-thirty in the morning by the time I finally open my eyes. So I'm getting a full night's rest, really. Sometimes ten, eleven hours of just... nothing. Just quiet, heavy sleep. So no, I'm not having any trouble staying asleep or waking up before I'm supposed to. I just stay right there in the bed until I'm done resting.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling like a bad person or that you have very little worth lately?\n\nPatient: Well, no... no, I wouldn't say that. A bad person? No. I mean, I've always tried to do right by people. When I was working at the packing plant, I always did my fair share of the work on the line. I never slacked off or left a mess for the next shift to clean up, which is more than I can say for some of the girls who worked there. There was this one girl, Brenda... well, she was always sneaking off to the breakroom to smoke those long, thin cigarettes she liked, leaving the rest of us to pick up the slack. But I never did that. I worked hard. I raised my family. I went to church on Sundays, at least until my husband passed and the drive just got to be a bit much for me on my own. \n\nAnd as for having little worth... well, I don't know about that either. I mean, I don't feel like I'm out here changing the world or anything, but I don't feel worthless. I just... I just feel like I'm here. Like that brown corduroy La-Z-Boy chair I was telling you about. It's just sitting there in the living room. It's not doing anything special, it's not going anywhere, but it's not a bad chair. It's just... resting. It has its place. \n\nI suppose I feel a bit like that. I'm just in my house, watching my programs, eating my oatmeal when I get around to it. I don't feel like a bad person for it. I don't feel guilty. I'm not sitting there thinking I'm a terrible burden or that I've done something wrong. I just don't have those kinds of thoughts, doctor. My mind is just... quiet. Like that still pond I mentioned before. There's no big waves of feeling bad about myself, no ripples of guilt. Just quiet. So no, I don't feel like a bad person or that I don't have any worth. I just feel like I'm taking up my little bit of space, and that's all.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Depressed? Well, no... I wouldn't use that word. Down? Not really. \n\nYou see, when I think of someone being depressed, I think of them crying all the time, or wringing their hands, or feeling real sorrowful about the state of the world. Like when they show those sad news stories on channel four, you know, with the poor folks who lost their homes in a flood or a tornado, and they're just weeping on camera. I don't feel like that at all. I don't feel like crying. In fact, I don't really feel much of anything, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. \n\nThe days just sort of... roll by. Like I was saying about sitting in my chair. I wake up, I eventually have my oatmeal, I watch my programs. The Price is Right is on in the mornings, though I'll tell you, it really hasn't been the same since Bob Barker left, bless his heart. Drew Carey tries his best, he really does, and he seems like a nice enough man, but it's just different now. But I watch it anyway, and the time just passes. I don't feel sad while I'm watching it. I don't feel happy, either. It's just a long stretch of quiet in my head. \n\nSo no, I don't feel down most of the day. I'm not sitting in the living room feeling blue or feeling sorry for myself. I just... exist. Kind of like a piece of furniture in the room. The lamp isn't sad, the coffee table isn't sad. They're just there, taking up space. That's how I feel from the time I get up until the time I go back to my Sealy mattress. Just there. So I wouldn't say I'm depressed at all, doctor. Just very, very quiet.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had any period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Two weeks? Well, let me think on that... no. No, I don't believe I have. I mean, life hasn't always been a bowl of cherries, you understand. When my husband passed away—oh, it’s been a good number of years now—well, naturally I was grieving. Anyone would be. We had his service over at the church, the one with the beautiful stained glass windows that face east so the morning sun comes right through during the early service. \n\nThe ladies from the church auxiliary, they brought over so many dishes... casseroles and baked ziti and a lovely green bean dish with those crispy fried onions on top. I actually had to ask my neighbor, Helen, if I could borrow some space in her chest freezer down in her basement because my little icebox in the kitchen was just bursting at the seams. But even then, you know, with all that grief, I wasn't just sitting around feeling depressed all day every day for two straight weeks. I had things to do. I had to make the arrangements, I had to sort through his clothes, and I had to write out all those thank-you cards by hand. I went down to the pharmacy and bought a special pen just for that, a nice one with blue ink, because black just felt a little too gloomy. You just... you just keep moving. \n\nAnd even before that, back when I was at the packing plant, there simply wasn't time to be down. You clocked in, you did your shift, you came home and made supper for the family. Usually a meatloaf on Tuesdays, or a pot roast if it was a Sunday. Folks like me just didn't have the luxury of taking two whole weeks to just sit and feel down about things. You put one foot in front of the other, you pay your bills, you wash your clothes. So, no, doctor, looking back over all my years, I can't say I've ever had a spell like what you're describing. I've always just carried on."
